synopsis: In 1909, Emily Wilde, a prickly scholar of faeries, travels to a remote Scandinavian village to study its fae, followed by her charming rival Wendell.
review:
This was an utterly enchanting read that captivated me with its quiet, steady charm. Instead of the high-stakes intensity you might find in epic fantasy, this book offers something equally compelling—a gentle yet deeply immersive journey into a world steeped in folklore and magic.

The dark fairytale vibes reminded me of Grimm stories, but with a touch of academic intrigue that felt fresh and unique. The faeries are portrayed with a perfect balance of wonder and danger, and the academic focus throughout was such a refreshing twist—it gave the story a grounded, thoughtful quality that I really loved.

Reading this novel felt like curling up alongside the main character in her cozy hut, observing her fascinating exploration of the faerie realm. The dynamic between the two main characters added warmth and humor to the story, and the world-building around the town and its people was one of the most delightful aspects.

This book is like a warm cup of tea on a cold day—comforting, magical, and utterly delightful. I’d recommend it to anyone who loves folklore, immersive worlds, and stories that wrap you up in their charm without needing to shout for your attention.

title: Gideon the Ninth
author: Tamsyn Muir
synopsis: An indentured swordswoman is forced to serve her rival, a necromancer, in deadly trials in a decaying palace. Funny and gothic.
review:
This has been an absolute delight to read and has quickly become one of my all-time favorite books. The world-building is beyond anything I’ve read in a while, with the necromancer techniques being so intricate and detailed that they pull you right into the story. Every chapter reveals something new and keeps you hooked.

The character progression is phenomenal. Gideon’s sarcastic, badass attitude pairs perfectly with Harrow’s complexity, and watching their relationship evolve is so satisfying. The blend of humor, dark themes, and mystery is just perfectly balanced. There’s a tension throughout the book that keeps you on the edge of your seat, and the reveals? Absolutely jaw-dropping.

It’s also one of those rare books that manages to mix sci-fi and fantasy in a way that feels seamless. I was completely immersed from beginning to end, and the twists are brilliantly executed. This book has everything I love: vivid characters, dark humor, and a world that feels like it could expand forever. I cannot recommend it enough!

author: Yōko Tawada
series: Scattered All Over the Earth, Book 1
synopsis: Hiruko's homeland, Japan, has disappeared, and she travels across Europe looking for anyone who still speaks her language.
review:
“Scattered All Over the Earth” had an intriguing concept, but it fell short in execution. The transphobia throughout the narrative was off-putting and unnecessary, and it distracted from the story. 

The world-building, which could have been a highlight, was shallow. The premise of countries disappearing was fascinating, but it was barely explored. Important details were glossed over, and interesting ideas were mentioned only to be abandoned without explanation.

The characters lacked depth, making it difficult to connect with them. The narrative was also bogged down by lengthy, seemingly irrelevant explanations that felt like they were trying to create meaning where there wasn’t any. These digressions were repeated throughout the book, but they never added real value or substance to the plot.

Overall, the book had potential but failed to develop its world and characters in a meaningful way. It aimed for depth but lacked the substance to support it.
